question: For a finite simple undirected graph with N vertices and adjacency matrix A: what does the entry (A^k)_{ij} count, what is a path between two vertices, and how can one decide from A alone whether the graph is connected?

claims.text: Galway notes Theorem 1.1.3: for the adjacency matrix A of a simple graph, the (i,j) entry of A^k (k a positive integer) is the number of walks of length k from v_i to v_j; proved by induction on k.

support.quote: Then the entry in the (i, j)-position of the matrix Ak is the number of walks of length k from vi to vj in G.

claims.text: Galway notes: the number of walks of length 2 from a vertex to itself equals the vertex degree, so trace(A^2) = 2|E|. This is the diagonal case that separates walks from paths.

support.quote: The number of walks of length 2 from a vertex to itself is just the number of edges at that vertex, or the vertex degree.

claims.text: Galway notes: the adjacency matrix has a 1 in position (i,j) if there is an edge from v_i to v_j; it is symmetric for undirected graphs and has zeros on the main diagonal unless there are loops.

support.locator: Definition 1.1.2 and Notes 1 and 2, printed p. 3
support.quote: The adjacency matrix is symmetric (i.e. equal to its transpose) if the graph is undirected.
The adjacency matrix has zeros on its main diagonal (unless the graph has loops).

claims.text: Gotti Proposition 2: for a graph (directed or undirected) on [n] with adjacency matrix A, there are (A^l)_jk walks of length l from j to k; proved by induction on l.

support.quote: For any j, k ∈ [n] and ` ∈ N, there are A`jk walks of length ` from j to k.

claims.text: Row sums of the adjacency matrix of a simple graph are the degrees: Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran state that the degree is the sum of the off-diagonal entries plus twice the diagonal entries, and for a simple graph the diagonal is zero.

support.quote: Degree of vi is equal to the sum of the off diagonal entries plus twice the diagonal entries.

claims.text: Gotti Proposition 3: a simple graph on [n] with adjacency matrix A is connected if and only if all entries of (I_n + A)^(n-1) are positive.

support.quote: Then G is connected if and only if all the entries of (In + A)n−1 are positive.

claims.text: Gotti's proof of Proposition 3 uses that connected vertices are joined by a path of length at most n - 1, so A^l_jk > 0 for some l in [n-1], plus the binomial identity for (I_n + A)^(n-1).

support.quote: any two distinct vertices j and k of G are connected by a path (of length at most n − 1)

claims.text: Bai Theorem 1: for a simple graph with n vertices, (A^k)_ij counts walks of length k from i to j; the note states it counts walks, not paths.

support.quote: Then for any two vertices i and j, the entry (Ak )ij counts the number of walks of length k from vertex i to vertex j.
counts walks — not paths.

claims.text: Bai defines a path as a walk where no vertex is repeated (except possibly first and last if it is a cycle).

support.quote: Path: A walk where no vertex is repeated (except possibly the first and last vertex if it’s a cycle).

claims.text: Bai Theorem 2: a simple graph with n vertices is connected if and only if (I + A)^(n-1) has all entries strictly positive.

support.quote: Then G is connected if and only if the matrix power (I + A)n−1 has all entries strictly positive.

claims.text: Bai's proof sketch says '(I + A)^(n-1) aggregates all paths of length <= n - 1', which is incomplete as stated: the entries count walks, and the sketch gives no walk-to-path step or binomial expansion. Bai has no sum form A + ... + A^(n-1).

support.quote: (I + A)n−1 aggregates all paths of length ≤ n − 1.

claims.text: Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran Theorem 2: with B = A + A^2 + ... + A^(n-1), the graph is connected if and only if b_ij is non-zero for i not equal to j (the sum form of the test).

support.quote: Then, AG is connected if and only if bij ≠ 0, when i ≠ j.

claims.text: Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran's proof of Theorem 2 reads b_ij as 'number of different paths of length less than n' and passes from a non-zero entry to a path without the walk-to-path lemma; the word 'path' is never defined in the paper.

support.quote: bij = number of different paths of length less than n from the vertex i to j.

claims.text: Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran Section 2.2 item 7 states that the (i,j) entry of A^m equals the number of walks of length m from v_i to v_j and that the least non-zero such m is the distance.

support.quote: The (i, j)th entry of Am G is equal to the number of walks of length m from vi to vj

claims.text: Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran Theorem 3: in a connected graph the distance between v_i and v_j is l iff l is the smallest integer with (A^l)_ij non-zero; its proof reads a non-zero entry as a path.

support.quote: The distance between two vertices vi and vj is equal to l if and only if l is the smallest integer such that (AlG)ij ≠ 0.

claims.text: Grinberg Definition 2.9.1: a walk is a vertex sequence (v_0, ..., v_k) with k >= 0 and consecutive vertices adjacent; a path is a walk whose vertices are distinct (simple graphs).

support.quote: A path (in G) means a walk (in G) whose vertices are distinct.
(with k ≥ 0)

claims.text: Grinberg Corollary 2.9.7: for a simple graph, if there is a walk of length k from u to v, there is a path from u to v of length at most k; this covers u = v.

support.quote: Assume that there is a walk from u to v of length k for some k ∈ N. Then, there is a path from u to v of length ≤ k.

claims.text: Grinberg: any path in an n-vertex graph has length at most n - 1, since a path of length k has k + 1 distinct vertices.

support.quote: any path from u to v must have length ≤ n − 1, where n is the number of vertices of G

claims.text: Grinberg Proposition 2.9.10: u and v are in the same component iff there is a path from u to v; Definition 2.9.12: a simple graph is connected if it has exactly one component. The proposition concerns walks and paths only, not trails.

support.quote: Then, u ≃G v if and only if there exists a path from u to v.
We say that G is connected if G has exactly one component.

claims.text: Grinberg's spanning-tree construction yields a breadth-first search tree in which the root-to-v tree path is a shortest path in G. This is the only BFS source read; it does not state BFS as a connectivity test.

support.quote: this spanning tree is called a breadth-first search (“BFS”) tree.

claims.text: The sum test A + ... + A^(N-1) and the test (I + A)^(N-1) are equivalent: both say every pair has a walk, hence a path, of length at most N - 1. No source read states both together; Gotti gives the binomial identity and Paramadevan the sum form, so the equivalence is to be proved in the paper.

Then, AG is connected if and only if bij ≠ 0, when i ≠ j.

claims.text: Distance from walk counts (derived): for distinct vertices n_i, n_j of a finite simple graph, the distance d(n_i, n_j) is the least k >= 1 with (A^k)_ij > 0 if some such k exists and infinity otherwise; d(n_i, n_i) = 0. Proof from the walk-counting theorem and the equality of the least walk length and the least path length (m2-5). Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran state it for connected graphs as their Theorem 3 (C46) and their proof reads a non-zero entry as a path.

support.quote: The distance between two vertices vi and vj is equal to l if and only if l is the smallest integer such that (AlG)ij ≠ 0.

claims.text: Walk-counting theorem: for a simple graph with adjacency matrix A and every integer k >= 0 (k >= 1 in the sources), (A^k)_ij is the number of walks of length k from n_i to n_j; proved by induction on k on the last-but-one vertex.

support.quote: Then the entry in the (i, j)-position of the matrix Ak is the number of walks of length k from vi to vj in G.
Then for any two vertices i and j, the entry (Ak )ij counts the number of walks of length k from vertex i to vertex j.
For any j, k ∈ [n] and ` ∈ N, there are A`jk walks of length ` from j to k.

claims.text: The number of walks of length 2 from a vertex to itself equals the vertex degree, so (A^2)_ii = d(n_i) and trace(A^2) = 2|E|.

support.quote: The number of walks of length 2 from a vertex to itself is just the number of edges at that vertex, or the vertex degree.

claims.text: Bai Theorem 1 is stated for simple graphs and the note says explicitly that the entry counts walks, not paths; Bai defines a path as a walk with no repeated vertex except possibly first and last in a cycle.

support.quote: counts walks — not paths.
Path: A walk where no vertex is repeated (except possibly the first and last vertex if it’s a cycle).

claims.text: Gotti Proposition 2 states walk counting for directed or undirected graphs; this supports a one-sentence remark that the theorem is not special to simple undirected graphs (directed graphs are out of scope).

support.quote: For any j, k ∈ [n] and ` ∈ N, there are A`jk walks of length ` from j to k.

claims.text: A path in a graph with N vertices has length at most N - 1, because a path of length k has k + 1 distinct vertices; hence if some walk joins two vertices, a path of length at most N - 1 joins them.

support.quote: any path from u to v must have length ≤ n − 1, where n is the number of vertices of G

claims.derivation: modules/m2.md, Section 5.3 (Corollary 2.3); script modules/m2-check.py, section 5 (longest path seen equals N - 1, never more)

claims.text: Grinberg Definition 2.10.1: a closed walk is a walk whose first vertex equals its last; a cycle is a closed walk (w_0, ..., w_k) with k >= 3 and w_0, ..., w_{k-1} distinct (simple graphs).

support.quote: A cycle of G means a closed walk (w0 , w1 , . . . , wk ) such that k ≥ 3 and such that the vertices w0 , w1 , . . . , wk−1 are distinct.

claims.text: Sum test (derived): G is connected if and only if every off-diagonal entry of B = A + A^2 + ... + A^(N-1) is positive. The entries of each A^k are non-negative integers, so B_ij > 0 exactly when some (A^k)_ij > 0 with 1 <= k <= N - 1, and Lemma M3.1 finishes. The statement is Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran Theorem 2; the proof here goes through the walk-to-path lemma that their proof omits (C43).

support.quote: Then, AG is connected if and only if bij ≠ 0, when i ≠ j.

claims.text: Power test (derived): G is connected if and only if (I + A)^(N-1) has no zero entry. Because I and A commute, (I + A)^(N-1) = sum over k = 0 to N-1 of C(N-1, k) A^k with every coefficient at least 1; off the diagonal this is positive exactly when B_ij > 0, and the k = 0 term makes every diagonal entry at least 1. The statement is Gotti Proposition 3 and Bai Theorem 2; the equivalence with the sum test is shown here (C52).

support.quote: Then G is connected if and only if all the entries of (In + A)n−1 are positive.
Then G is connected if and only if the matrix power (I + A)n−1 has all entries strictly positive.

claims.text: Three-vertex path graph G1 (edges v1v2, v2v3): A^2 has rows (1,0,1),(0,2,0),(1,0,1); A^3 has rows (0,2,0),(2,0,2),(0,2,0); B = A + A^2 has rows (1,1,1),(1,2,1),(1,1,1). (A^2)_11 = 1 counts the walk v1v2v1; (A^2)_13 = 1 counts v1v2v3; (A^2)_22 = 2 counts v2v1v2 and v2v3v2; (A^3)_12 = 2 counts v1v2v1v2 and v1v2v3v2. The only path from v1 to v1 is the single vertex v1 (length 0), so (A^2)_11 does not count paths. Computed by script.

Four-vertex path graph G3 (edges v1v2, v2v3, v3v4): A^2 has rows (1,0,1,0),(0,2,0,1),(1,0,2,0),(0,1,0,1); A^3 has rows (0,2,0,1),(2,0,3,0),(0,3,0,2),(1,0,2,0); B = A + A^2 + A^3 has rows (1,3,1,1),(3,2,4,1),(1,4,2,3),(1,1,3,1). The entry (1,4) of A and of A^2 is 0 and of A^3 is 1, counting the walk v1v2v3v4. Computed by script.

Reachability lemma (derived): for i different from j, a path from v_i to v_j exists iff (A^k)_ij > 0 for some k with 1 <= k <= N-1. Proof: a path of length k has k+1 distinct vertices so k <= N-1 (Grinberg Section 2.9.4), a path is a walk and the walk-counting theorem gives a positive entry; conversely a walk of length k gives a path of length at most k (Grinberg Corollary 2.9.7, proved in the paper as the lemma that every walk contains a path).

support.quote: Assume that there is a walk from u to v of length k for some k ∈ N. Then, there is a path from u to v of length ≤ k.

claims.text: The connectivity definition used (every two vertices are joined by a path) is equivalent to Grinberg's one-component definition, by his Proposition 2.9.10: u and v lie in the same component iff a path joins them.

support.quote: Then, u ≃G v if and only if there exists a path from u to v.

claims.text: Grinberg Definition 2.1.1: a simple graph is a pair (V, E), where V is a finite set and E is a subset of P2(V), the set of 2-element subsets of V; so there are no loops, at most one edge between two vertices, and the edge uv is the edge vu.

support.quote: A simple graph is a pair (V, E), where V is a finite set, and where E is a subset of P2 (V ).
